[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne is a large scale data center provider headquartered in Dallas, Texas. In 2016 CyrusOne purchased the Chicago Mercantile Exchanges original Aurora, Illinois data center from CME Group for roughly 130 million dollars, with CME Group continuing to operate its Globex matching engine on site under a 15 year lease. In November 2021, KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners agreed to acquire CyrusOne in an approximately 15 billion dollar deal, taking the company private, and that acquisition closed in 2022. CyrusOne has operated as a privately held company since, a company level ownership fact this registry had not previously recorded with a citable source. This specific row, PHX3, is one of five entries in this registry for this operators Chandler, Arizona campus on South Ellis Street. A datacentermap listing dedicated to PHX3, fetched fresh this session, gives 2305 South Ellis Street, Building 5, Chandler, Arizona 85286 as the street address. Direct per building fetches this session confirmed each PHX numbered building on this campus carries its own distinct street number and building number rather than sharing one unified campus address.

reading.body:
PHX3 is one of five buildings in CyrusOne's Chandler campus on South Ellis Street, located at 2305 South Ellis Street Building 5 in Chandler, Arizona. The campus as a whole publishes 169 MW of total IT capacity across all buildings, though the individual capacity of PHX3 itself is not confirmed in published specifications. The facility holds TIA 942 Class 4 certification and Energy Star Data Center Certification at select facilities on the campus, qualifying it for high-availability enterprise and mission-critical workloads.

At the campus level, 169 MW of IT capacity represents roughly 4,200 racks assuming 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, or could support roughly 1,400 racks at 120 kW per rack, typical for dense accelerator clusters. The Chandler campus ranks fifth among Arizona's facilities by published capacity and accounts for roughly one-third of the 512 MW of published data center capacity in the state, though Arizona has 56 mapped facilities total, most of which publish no capacity figure.

This facility matters to the grid and power planning in Arizona but sits in a state with limited published capacity disclosure. Only four Arizona facilities publish megawatt figures, making the actual scale of AI infrastructure investment in the region opaque and the role this campus plays in state power demand difficult to assess without operator disclosures.
